claims.text: A conformal nanoscale silver-based surface layer will form an in situ lubricious tribofilm during sliding.
The silver-derived tribofilm will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate over a broad temperature range.
The initial refractory multi-principal-element alloy has a single-phase microstructure.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous microstructure.
The untreated alloy has no intrinsic lubricious secondary phase.
Physical-vapor deposition followed by thermal annealing will produce a thin, well-adhered silver layer with improved interfacial bonding.
The treatment will remain effective during sliding in moderately humid ambient air from near room temperature to approximately 600 °C.
Silver remains solid and stable throughout the proposed temperature range up to approximately 600 °C.
The treatment produces nanoscale silver particles and a continuous interfacial silver network at the alloy surface.
Mechanical sliding shears and spreads the silver into a continuous tribofilm.
The continuous silver tribofilm reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and adhesive interactions.
Reducing direct contact and adhesive interactions lowers wear.
Ductile silver accommodates interfacial strain without cracking.
Refractory multi-principal-element alloys can exhibit dynamic twin formation.
Silver treatment will lower coefficient of friction by approximately 20–40% relative to the untreated alloy.
Silver treatment will lower wear rate by approximately 30–50% relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy has higher friction and wear because of direct asperity contact and limited formation of a self-adaptive lubricious surface.
An excessively thin or non-uniform silver layer will compromise lubrication effectiveness.
Temperatures approaching or exceeding silver's melting point will compromise the intervention.
Oxidizing environments can rapidly degrade the silver tribofilm and compromise its effectiveness.
